notes:
**Ask your broker what it actually gives you.** Strategies now opens
with a data check: it asks your own account for a year of candles on
the index, the futures contract, a live option and whatever equity or
commodity you watch, then tells you exactly what came back and what can
honestly be tested with it. Every claim the app makes about a backtest
now rests on that measurement instead of an assumption.

**The strategy builder speaks plainly.** Whatever you pick, the top of
the screen says what you built in one sentence â€” "When NIFTY's 9-candle
average crosses above its 21-candle average, buy 1 lot of NIFTY
futures. Sell again at 1% profit, at 0.5% loss, or before the market
closes." The two numbers that decide whether an idea is worth trying
are money now, not jargon: what it sets aside to hold, and what each
buy-and-sell costs in charges.

**Options work end to end.** Choose a call or a put, how far from the
money, and which expiry. Your rule watches the index; when it fires the
app buys that actual contract at the real premium, with the stop and
target set on the premium. A backtest shows you WHEN the rule fired and
puts no rupee figure on the option â€” those strikes have expired and
nobody can price them any more â€” so the real answer comes from running
it forward on paper.

**Futures roll themselves.** A rule built on the August contract moves
to the next one when August expires, keeping its history and its caps,
and never while a position is open.

**Two fixes underneath.** Backtests were charging a flat 0.35% of
turnover when a broker charges about a sixth of that â€” every result was
buried under costs that were never real. And positions were being held
overnight in a test while the deployed version squares off at the bell,
so the report described trades the app would never place.
